title: Evidence of Cosmic Impact at Abu Hureyra, Syria at the Younger Dryas Onset (~12.8 ka): High-temperature melting at >2200 °C ...

nodes.title: Michael W. Gaultois 12 & Allen West 13*
nodes.summary: Abstract and introduction of a 2020 Scientific Reports paper on Abu Hureyra, Syria (Younger Dryas Onset, ~12.8 ka). It reports high-temperature meltglass (>2200 °C), nanodiamonds, microspherules, and charcoal in the YDB, with elevated Ir, Pt, Ni, Co suggesting meteoritic mixing. Glass shows carbon-infused plant imprints and melted quartz, chromite, and magnetite; low water content and remanent magnetism argue against hut fires, lightning, volcanism, or anthropogenesis, supporting a cosmic airburst. It reviews the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis, its climate and cultural effects, and the opposing Thy et al. heating-experiment view, and lists the paper's four research questions.

nodes.title: Site Setting, Geology, and Age
nodes.summary: Describes Abu Hureyra, a tell settlement in northern Syria on the Euphrates, now beneath Lake Assad. Covers local geology (Eocene chalky limestone, chert, marls, Quaternary alluvium) and excavated charcoal-rich living surfaces containing meltglass, Fe- and Si-rich spherules, nanodiamonds, and carbon spherules. These surfaces are Bayesian-dated to 12825 ± 55 cal BP (Younger Dryas boundary age). Impact materials appear in three trenches (D, E, G) up to 175 m apart.

nodes.title: Results and Interpretations
Abu Hureyra meltglass.
nodes.summary: Describes Abu Hureyra (AH) meltglass from a Younger Dryas boundary site in Syria: its analysis methods (microscopy, SEM-EDS, microprobe, FTIR), morphology (mostly 1-2 mm fragments, vesicular, often float, with mineral inclusions and crystalline linings), and composition (Ca-rich aluminosilicate, similar to local sediment, high carbon from carbonates). Notes the glass is isotropic under crossed polarizers, consistent with amorphous glass, and compares it to other YDB glasses and prior studies.

nodes.title: Furnace and torch heating experiments.
nodes.summary: Furnace and torch heating experiments (1100–1850 °C) on Abu Hureyra (AH) sediment and plant-imprinted AH glass test whether local melting formed the glass. Glass fragments melt at 1200–1300 °C, a minimum exposure temperature. Bulk sediment forms glass similar to AH glass near 1700 °C; partial quartz melting begins ~1300 °C, aided by fluxes. Results give a solidus of 1200–1300 °C, contradicting Thy et al.'s maximum-temperature claim. Figure 2 shows AH glass spheroids and fragments with chromite and monazite inclusions.

nodes.title: AH meltglass with carbon-rich siliceous plant imprints.
key_items: AH meltglass with carbon-rich siliceous plant imprints.
nodes.summary: Plant-imprinted AH meltglass: about 40% of pieces show carbon-infused ribbed impressions matching plant stems and leaves, with charcoal inclusions indicating biomass burning. Imprints average about 80 wt.% SiO2 and 20 wt.% carbon, unlike the Ca-rich non-imprinted glass. SEM reveals a three-layered morphology (Ca-rich matrix, silicified plant layer, transition), interpreted as molten glass fusing to plant material. Associated with magnetic spherules, nanodiamonds, and Ni, Co, Ir, Pt peaks. Reflectance-derived temperatures: about 421 C for embedded carbon, about 391 C for loose charcoal, showing glass stayed hotter than the charcoal it enclosed.

nodes.title: Silicon-rich minerals as temperature indicators.
nodes.summary: Describes silica (SiO2) varieties found in AH glass, identified by light microscopy and SEM-EDS: (i) thin vitreous or glassy amorphous SiO2 coatings called lechatelierite; (ii) subrounded melted glass objects that are nearly 100 wt.% SiO2; (iii) partially to fully melted quartz grains. These silicon-rich minerals serve as temperature indicators.

nodes.title: Melted amorphous silica (SiO2 as lechatelierite).
Silicon-rich minerals as temperature indicators.
nodes.summary: Describes AH meltglass from a Scientific Reports study (2020). Surfaces and vesicles are coated with lechatelierite (amorphous SiO2, 88.3-98.7 wt.%), with minor MgO, Al2O3, K2O, CaO, FeO. Sinuous flow marks show low viscosity before rapid cooling; moire-like textures form on cooling, distorted by surface irregularities and conforming to cracks. Figures show silicified and carbon-infused plant imprints, charred organics (~421 C reflectance temperature), partially melted quartz grains (melting point ~1720 C, flux-adjusted ~1520 C), and SEM/EDS maps. Coatings likely formed by vaporization/deposition of quartz or silica-rich plants, inferred melting range 1200-1300 C.

nodes.title: Melted quartz grains (SiO2).
nodes.summary: Melted quartz grains (SiO2, melting ~1720 °C) in AH meltglass were examined by light microscopy, SEM-EDS, and microprobe, revealing fully and partially melted grains with diffusion zones. Oxygen-deficient mixtures suggest native Si, possibly from reducing conditions or impact. Melted zircon, chromite/titanomagnetite grains, a shattered quartz breccia (Meteor Crater analogy), and a 1040-μm quartz grain possibly boiling at ~2230 °C are described. Furnace experiments and ternary diagrams support temperature estimates; reference quartz checks validate the Si/O measurements.

nodes.title: Ca silicate (wollastonite).
nodes.summary: Describes wollastonite (CaSiO3), a calcium silicate with a triclinic crystal system that often forms star-like crystals. It appeared on the outer surfaces and vesicle walls of AH glass, but never inside the glass or on plant imprints. Wollastonite melts at 1540 °C, with an estimated flux-mediated melting point of about 1340 °C.

Melted amorphous silica (lechatelierite) in AH meltglass: surfaces and vesicles coated with SiO2 (88-99 wt.%) showing flow marks, moire textures, and plant imprints, implying melting at about 1200-1300 C. Partially melted quartz grains (melting ~1720 C, flux-adjusted ~1520 C) show diffusion zones, possible native Si, melted zircon and chromite, and a quartz grain possibly boiling near 2230 C. Wollastonite (CaSiO3, melts ~1540 C) occurs only on outer surfaces and vesicle walls.

nodes.title: Zirconium-rich minerals.
nodes.summary: Describes melted zircon grains in aluminosilicate AH meltglass. An 8-μm zircon grain's SEM-EDS composition is given (Zr 46.1, Si 15.8, O 36.0, Hf ~2.1 wt.%). Zircon melts near 1775 °C, or ~1575 °C with flux. Full melting removes its euhedral shape and diffuses it into the glass, with zircon content in the matrix falling from 100 to 90, 70, then 0 wt.%. The text ends mid-sentence about a glass surface.

nodes.title: Chromium-rich minerals.
nodes.summary: Excavated AH glass contains three Cr-rich minerals identified by SEM-EDS: isovite (highest Cr, 67.4 wt.%), chromite, and chrome-magnetite (Cr 11.3 wt.%), plus chromferide (lowest Cr, 11.0 wt.%), a rare mineral also found at El'gygytgyn Crater. Some grains are intergrowths of chromferide and isovite. A chromium-magnetite grain embedded in the glass surface shows molten flow marks from aerodynamic deformation. Fe-rich globules (FeO and iron silicides) cover original glass surfaces and vesicles.

nodes.title: Iron-rich minerals.
key_items: Melted iron with platinum and iridium.; Melted iron silicide.
Melted iron with platinum and iridium.
nodes.summary: Describes iron-rich, nickel-rich, platinum/iridium-bearing, silicide, sulfide, monazite, and magnetic-property findings in Abu Hureyra (AH) meltglass from the Younger Dryas boundary layer. Covers SEM-EDS observations of Fe globules, magnetite, titanomagnetite, native Fe, and FeS (troilite); NiFe minerals (kamacite, taenite, awaruite, Ni-magnetite); PGE-rich grains; Fe silicides (Fe3Si, FeSi, Fe2Si); melted monazite and quartz; and remanent magnetism and water content comparisons. Infers highly reducing, carbon-rich vesicle conditions and temperatures from ~1500 to ~2623 °C.

nodes.title: Sulfide minerals.
key_items: Melted Fe sulfide (troilite).; Melted Titanium sulfide.
nodes.summary: Describes sulfide minerals in AH glass fragments. Troilite (FeS, about 64 wt.% Fe, 36 wt.% S) forms globules found only on surfaces and inside vesicles, likely by vapor deposition. Melted titanium sulfide (TiS) occurs with melted magnetite and other high-temperature minerals. TiS and TiP presence indicates high-temperature melting under highly reducing, oxygen-poor conditions.

nodes.title: Rare-earth-rich phosphate (monazite).
key_items: Melted iron with platinum and iridium; Melted iron silicide
Melted iron with platinum and iridium
nodes.summary: Describes melted monazite (a rare-earth phosphate) inside AH glass vesicles, identified by SEM-EDS. The grain has a faint outline but no distinct boundary due to melting and diffusion into the glass, and it surrounds part of a melted quartz grain. Gas bubbles in the monazite suggest outgassing of oxygen at about 2230 °C. This indicates rapid cooling from a superheated liquid, with oxygen-deficient liquid forming at a blocking temperature. The quartz also contains small vesicles, suggesting it reached its boiling point of about 2230 °C.

nodes.title: Remanent magnetism as a formation criterion.
key_items: Remanent magnetism of AH magnetic spherules.; Remanent magnetism of YDB meltglass.
Remanent magnetism of AH magnetic spherules.
nodes.summary: Describes remanent magnetism as a test for whether Fe-rich spherules and meltglass from Abu Hureyra and YDB formed from lightning or impact. Remanent magnetization records Earth's field at cooling (Curie point). Abu Hureyra spherules show no lightning-range remanence and a consistent direction, indicating geomagnetic acquisition. Meltglass shows normal single-component magnetization, though results are complex: plasma effects may reduce remanence, and variable values could indicate lightning or a fireball depending on cooling location.

nodes.title: Water content as a temperature indicator.
key_items: Remanent magnetism as a formation criterion.
Remanent magnetism of AH magnetic spherules
nodes.summary: Covers water content of Abu Hureyra (AH) glass as a temperature indicator: FTIR measurements show 222–460 ppm H2O (n=19), implying high-temperature formation with volatile outgassing. Also lists high-temperature minerals on AH glass surfaces and vesicle walls (chromite, monazite, zircon, magnetite, wollastonite, iron phases, etc.) with equilibrium and flux melting temperatures, oxygen fugacity buffers, and notes flux melting points about 200 °C below equilibrium.

Covers Abu Hureyra (Younger Dryas boundary, Syria) meltglass: morphology and Ca-rich aluminosilicate composition; furnace/torch experiments showing local melting near 1200-1300 C solidus; carbon-rich plant imprints with reflectance temperatures (~391-421 C); lechatelierite, partially melted quartz, zircon, chromium minerals (isovite, chromite, chromferide), Fe/Ni/PGE phases, silicides, troilite, TiS, monazite; remanent magnetism pointing to geomagnetic acquisition rather than lightning; and low water content (222-460 ppm) indicating high-temperature formation.

nodes.title: Discussion and Implications
Laboratory experiments.
nodes.summary: Discussion of Abu Hureyra (AH) glass, which contains high-temperature minerals (chromite, monazite, zircon, quartz, magnetite, iron silicides; melting points ~1410-2265 °C). Covers lab heating experiments: zircon decomposes to baddeleyite at ~1500-1700 °C; chromite and Fe-rich globules survive ~1700-1850 °C; Fe-Si silicides form in carbon-rich, low-oxygen conditions. Charcoal reflectance indicates carbon temperatures over 800 °C lower than surrounding melt, and low water content resembles AH glass, suggesting plant material cooled the glass rapidly.

nodes.title: Potential formation by non-impact processes.
nodes.summary: Argues Abu Hureyra (AH) glass was not formed by cosmic impact via biomass burning, wildfires, lightning, anthropogenic or volcanic processes. Biomass slag lacks >2000 °C melted grains; wildfire reflectance temperatures are unreliable for impacts; fulgurites and volcanic obsidian show strong remanent magnetism unlike AH glass; FTIR shows AH glass water content far lower. AH glass is compared to 1945 Trinity trinitite: similar melted quartz, Fe silicides, native Fe and carbon-linked formation, suggesting nuclear-detonation-like conditions. Age and burial preclude anthropogenesis.

nodes.title: Comparison to known impact meltglass.
nodes.summary: Compares Abu Hureyra (AH) glass to known impact meltglass using SEM-EDS and microprobe analysis across sites: Australasian tektites (melted quartz), Dakhleh Oasis (melted zircon), Meteor Crater (melted chromite, Fe-rich inclusions), and Chasico. Notes Ries, Darwin, Houghton, Monturaqui, and Zhaminshin craters. Remanent magnetism varies from weak to strong versus AH. Water content: tektites typically under 500 ppm; studied samples range 78-1036 ppm, wider than AH's 222-460 ppm.

nodes.title: Similar proxies from other YDB sites.
nodes.summary: Compares Abu Hureyra (AH) YDB proxies with other YDB sites (Blackville, Melrose) using microscopy, SEM-EDS, neutron activation, remanent magnetism, and Pt, Ir, Ni, Co, Cr abundances. Remanent magnetism suggests spherules and meltglass were not lightning-formed. Dendritic Fe-rich minerals match across sites; internal Fe-rich textures at Blackville and Melrose imply slower cooling. Native iron indicates low oxygen fugacity. Table 2 shows AH material resembles impact and cosmic airbursts, unlike anthropogenic, biomass, lightning, volcanic, or wildfire material. Elemental enrichments match about 30 other YDB sites, attributed to a cosmic impact.

The section covers Abu Hureyra (AH) glass, which contains high-temperature minerals. Lab heating experiments show zircon decomposition, chromite and Fe-globule survival, and Fe-Si silicide formation under low oxygen. Charcoal reflectance and low water content suggest rapid cooling by plant material. Non-impact origins (biomass, wildfire, lightning, volcanic, anthropogenic) are argued against, and AH is compared to Trinity trinitite. It is compared with known impact meltglass and other YDB sites, whose proxies and elemental enrichments point to a cosmic impact.

nodes.title: Conclusions
nodes.summary: Abu Hureyra glass study concludes its meltglass lacks high-temperature minerals inside, implying internal temperatures near 1250 C versus ambient at least 1750 to over 2600 C. Heating experiments map mineral melting ranges. Natural origins except impact melt and tektites are excluded. Evidence supports a hypervelocity airburst or impact about 12,800 years ago, part of the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis involving comet debris clusters causing coeval impacts across more than 14,000 km.

nodes.title: Methods
key_items: Laboratory melting experiments.; SEM-EDS analyses.; Carbon reflectance.; Remanent magnetism.; Transmission FTIR and water content.
nodes.summary: Methods for a Younger Dryas boundary study of Abu Hureyra: laboratory melting experiments on sediment and plant-imprinted glass (alumina crucibles, box furnace, type B thermocouple); SEM-EDS analyses; carbon reflectance; remanent magnetism via SQUID magnetometer on seven samples; transmission FTIR for water content; electron microprobe analyses. Data availability notes the site is submerged under Lake Assad, with no bulk YDB sediment left, and meltglass archived in London. Also includes publication dates and a long reference list (1-79) on Younger Dryas impact evidence, nanodiamonds, spherules, melting, magnetism, and water in glass.

summary: A 2020 Scientific Reports study of Abu Hureyra, Syria, at the Younger Dryas onset (~12.8 ka) reports high-temperature meltglass (>2200 °C), nanodiamonds, microspherules, and charcoal, with elevated Ir, Pt, Ni, and Co suggesting a cosmic airburst. Site geology, Bayesian dating (12825 ± 55 cal BP), lab melting and mineral analyses, magnetism, and low water content are covered, with non-impact origins ruled out. It reviews the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis, the opposing Thy et al. view, methods, conclusions, references, and acknowledgements.
